Introduction
First editor's draft
In the field of data management, even moreso with the advent of big data, analysis of data is usually performed through the use of numerous mathematical and other functions. Implementations of programming languages (for example, programming languages C and Java™) are often accompanied by large libraries of functions that can be invoked by applications written using those programming languages.
First editor's draft
For numerous reasons, both historical and personal taste, the function libraries associated with one programming language are often significantly different than those associated with other programming languages. Although such differences can be explained in part by the intent of each programming language, having those differences often results in the selection of a given programming language for reasons other than the expressiveness of the language itself in favor of the functions available in the function libraries of that language. One (partial) solution to that issue is standardization of function libraries for use in data management as a whole.
First editor's draft
As organizations have become more aware of the implications of big data as it affects their operations, the need for more modern, more advanced techniques to analyze and manage that data is become more apparent. The term advanced analytics (sometimes called next-generation analytics) refers to the tools used to maximize the value those organizations must extract from their data. Primary among those tools are comprehensive libraries of functions that are invoked by applications and by data scientists working with the data.
First editor's draft
The functions defined in the parts of ISO/IEC 29075 are specified in a manner to encourage their use by applications written (in whole or in part) using ISO/IEC 9075 and ISO/IEC 39075. Naturally, they may be used by applications written in other programming languages, although the details of their implementations may require adaptation to suit the function calling mechanisms of those languages.

Concepts
Specification of function libraries
First editor's draft
A function library is a collection of software routines that may be invoked from a software program. In general, the functions belonging to a specific function library are related in some conceptual or implementation-dependent manner. In ISO/IEC 29075, a number of functions that compute statistical information about data supplied to those functions; specifies a function library defining a number of statistical functions.
First editor's draft
Functions in a particular function library sometimes operate on values of a specific declared type, or they sometimes return values of a specific declared type. The definition of a particular function library specifies the declared type or types of values supplied to invocations of each function and the declared type or types of the results of invoking each function.
First editor's draft
In each part of ISO/IEC 29075, every function has a unique function name. Implementations of each of those functions may, in some circumstances, result in more than one actual software function. That may, in turn, affect the manner in which each function invocation is coded in a particular programming language. This document does not make any provisions for such circumstances.

Specification of functions in libraries
First editor's draft
There are many programming languages in use, and each such language has its own specifications for the definition of functions that can be invoked from programs written in that language and its own specifications of the manner in which such functions are invoked. These specifications include how functions are named, how those names are expressed, the manner in which function parameters are defined (including the names and data types of those parameters), the way in which arguments to function invocations must be related to parameters, and so forth.
First editor's draft

Notations
Function specifications
First editor's draft
Each function provided in each part of ISO/IEC 29075 is specified in several sections of text, some of which use programming language notations. Those sections are:
First editor's draft
Function Purpose
First editor's draft
Function Signature
First editor's draft
Parameter Definitions
First editor's draft
Results
First editor's draft
Argument Considerations
First editor's draft
Formal Definition
First editor's draft
Exceptions and Warnings
First editor's draft
Each of these sections are explained in the following Subclauses.
Function Purpose section
First editor's draft
A Purpose section specifies the purpose of the function in a short statement.
Function Signature section
First editor's draft
A Signature section specifies the name of the function that is used to invoke the function, the number of parameters used by invocations of the function, the names and data types of each parameter, the number of results returned by the function when invoked, and the names and data types of each such result.
Parameter Definition sections
First editor's draft
A Parameter Definition section specifies the purpose or meaning of each formal parameter to the function and provides additional details, including possible restrictions or limitations, about the parameters. For each parameter, this section specifies whether an invocation of the function must provide a value for the parameter, or whether provision of a value is optional. For parameters that are optional, this section specifies the effect of no value is provided when the function is invoked.
Results sections
First editor's draft
A Results section specifies the purpose or meaning of each value that can be returned from the function. It also specifies, for each possible result, whether or not the result is always provided in response to a function invocation. For results that are not always provided, this section also specifies the interpretation of the absence of the result.
Argument Considerations section
First editor's draft
An Arguments Considerations section discusses special considerations associated with each arguments used when invoking the function. Such considerations might include what the range of acceptable values are, interactions between the values of two or more arguments, and when an application should choose one combination of arguments and values over a different combination.
Formal Definition section
First editor's draft
A Formal Definition section specifies the precise semantics of the function. Some formal definitions might specify those semantics using a brief natural language description. Others might do so through the use of pseudo-code written in a semi-formal manner or even in natural language. Still others might specify semantics using mathematical notations, formulae, etc.
Exceptions and Warnings section
First editor's draft
An Exceptions and Warnings section identifies every kind of error or warning that a routine invocation might encounter and specifies the exact manner in which the error or warning is indicated to the invoker (including, when appropriate, the error code or warning code) and suggests actions that an application might attempt to resolve the error or warning.
Conformance section
First editor's draft
A Conformance section specifies what features of ISO/IEC 29075 apply to the function. Generally, this section contains statements of the form, Without Feature FLnnn, function my_function shall not be invoked.
First editor's draft
Data type specifications
First editor's draft
Parameters of functions always have a data type, as do arguments of function invocations that correspond to those parameters. In general, the data type of an argument of a function invocation is a subtype of the data type of the corresponding parameter of the function being invoked.
First editor's draft
More specifically, a parameter declaration in a function signature specifies the declared type of the parameter, while the run-time data type of the corresponding argument, known as the most-specific type, is the precise data type of the value provided for the argument.
First editor's draft
For example, if a parameter declaration in a function signature specifies the data type of that parameter as integer, a valid argument value might be 42, which could be represented as an 8-bit integer, a 16-bit integer, a 32-bit integer, or even a 2-digit decimal value.
First editor's draft
All argument values shall be convertible, without loss of information, to the declared types of their corresponding parameters.
First editor's draft
In this document, the following notations are used for declared typesImplementations of the various functions defined in the parts of ISO/IEC 29075 shall precisely specify the declared types of parameters of those functions based on the underlying programming language, operating system, and hardware platform used:
First editor's draft
Integer — an exact numeric data type having scale 0; the precision of the data type is not further specified by this document. An example of an Integer value is 13.
First editor's draft
Decimal — an exact numeric data type having a scale other than 0; the precision of the data type is not further specified by this document. An example of a Decimal value is 159.72.
First editor's draft
Real — an approximate numeric data type, the representation of which specifies a mantissa and an exponent; in this document, the precisions of the mantissa and exponent are not further specified, and the exponent shall be interpreted as powers of 10. An example of a Real value is 314159E1.
First editor's draft
Character — a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters; in this document, no specification is made regarding the Unicode transformation format (e.g., UTF-8 or UTF-16). An example of a Character value is This is a string.
First editor's draft
Datetime — a value representing a date in the Gregorian calendar, a time of day, or both, that is representable in the notation specified in . Datetime values are permitted, but not required, to contain time zone components. An example of a Datetime value is 2001-09-11T11:30:40.6.
First editor's draft
Period — a value representing a span of time (including without limitation a span of dates) that is representable in the notation specified in . An example of a Period value is P1DT5H3M25.75S.
First editor's draft
Boolean — a value representing a true or false condition; the representation of Boolean values is not further specified in this document.
First editor's draft Other declared types will be added as required.
Status codes
First editor's draft
Some status codes are potentially returned by every (or almost every) function defined by any part of ISO/IEC 29075. These are specified in . Status codes that are returned only by some or all functions defined in a particular part of ISO/IEC 29075 are specified by an analogous table contained in that particular part.
First editor's draft
Functions defined by ISO/IEC 29075 always return a status code that indicates whether the function completed successfully and returned a (meaningful) result; completed successfully, but did not return a meaningful result; completed successfully, but with a warning that indicates the results might not be meaningful; or was unable to complete successful, accompanied by an indication of the reason for failure.
First editor's draft
The status code returned by functions defined in ISO/IEC 29075 is always an integer.

Conformance
Claims of conformance to ISO/IEC 29075
First editor's draft
Claims of conformance to ISO/IEC 29075 shall always include a claim of conformance to . A claim of conformance to does not necessarily imply a claim of conformance to any particular feature defined in any part of ISO/IEC 29075.
First editor's draft
In addition, claims of conformance to ISO/IEC 29075 shall include a claim of conformance to one or more features identified in parts of ISO/IEC 29075 other this document. Features identified in other parts of ISO/IEC 29075 are generally identified by feature codes that begin with the letter "F" (which implied Function library), followed by a second letter that indicates the part of ISO/IEC 29075 in which the feature is defined, followed by three digits that identify the specific feature within the identified part.
First editor's draft
Some features defined in other parts of ISO/IEC 9075 require conforming implementation of a single function, while other features require conforming implementation of several functions that must all be provided.

First editor's draft
